entry.title: Safely Test a MySQL 5.7 -> 8.0 Upgrade on Azure
entry.summary:
Upgrading a production database? Don't make production your test environment. A safer approach is to restore production to a separate Azure MySQL server, test the upgrade there, and only then upgrade production. Production MySQL 5.7 ↓ Restore to separate test server ↓ Verify server ↓ Run MySQL Upgrade Checker ↓ Fix compatibility issues ↓ Upgrade test server to MySQL 8.0 ↓ Test application ↓ Upgrade production
Create a separate Azure MySQL server from a recent production backup or point-in-time restore. Your production database remains untouched while you test the upgrade. Connect to the test server, not production, using MySQL Shell: \connect user@server.mysql.database.azure.com \js
Verify where you're connected: SELECT @@hostname, @@version;
Then run the Upgrade Checker: util.checkForServerUpgrade({ targetVersion: "8.0" })
The checker identifies known compatibility issues that should be addressed before upgrading. Important: The Upgrade Checker is not a replacement for application testing. Once the reported issues are addressed, upgrade the test server to MySQL 8.0. Then point your application to the test database and test: Queries Migrations APIs Queues and jobs Authentication Stored procedures/events, if used Application functionality Performance If the test upgrade succeeds and your application behaves correctly, prepare your production backup and maintenance plan, then perform the production upgrade. Restore → Check → Fix → Upgrade → Test → Upgrade production The key rule is simple: Never make production your first upgrade test. 🚀

entry.summary: Containers limit blast radius. They do not prevent an autonomous coding agent from reading a secret in one tool call and exfiltrating it via an outbound network call in the next, all within the same approved session. The question is how to build a gate that does not break legitimate agent workflows while blocking destructive operations, and what happens when the gate itself fails. entry.title: Portless: Stable .localhost URLs for Agent Workflows
entry.summary: Local development usually means localhost:3000, localhost:8080, and a mental map of which port belongs to which service. AI agents struggle with this. They cannot reliably track dynamic port assignments across restarts, and they cannot predict which port a framework will choose when you spin up a new service. Portless replaces port numbers with stable .localhost URLs. Instead of http://localhost:3000, you get https://myapp.localhost. The tool handles TLS, port assignment, and framework-specific CLI flag injection so your services bind to the right port without manual configuration.
